newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel halts talks, world pleads they continue.
newsitem.headline: Israel halts talks, world pleads they continue.

text.p: Israel called a halt to peace talks with the Palestinians after a suicide bombing killed 15 people, despite calls from world leaders to press on with negotiations.
Police said two bombers, who were among the dead, detonated bombs in briefcases at Jewish west Jerusalem's Mahane Yehuda market on Wednesday. About 170 people were wounded.
A leaflet issued in the name of the Moslem militant Hamas group claimed responsibility. Hamas gave Israel until 1800 GMT on Sunday to free all Palestinian prisoners.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, on her way back from an Asian tour, told reporters Israeli Prime Minisiter Benjamin Netanyahu had pledged to keep the peace process alive.

"We talked about the importance of returning to the peace process and I urged him to do so and he said he understood the importance of returning to the peace process," she said. "He did say he would return to the process."
Netanyahu convened Israel's ministerial committee on national security after the bombing. More than five hours later, his spokesman Shai Bazak announced its decisions.
"At this stage no steps will be taken (in the peace process) so long as the Palestinian Authority doesn't take steps it committed to," Bazak told Israel Radio.
He said Israel "sees the Palestinian Authority as responsible for acts of terrorism" because it had not kept obligations to wage "war against terrorist organisations."
"The cabinet has directed the army and security forces to take a series of steps against the Palestinian terrorist organisations. I will not elaborate on that subject," he added.
Israel had already sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip and restricted Palestinians to their home districts.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters after Bazak's statement that the authority had combatted militants opposed to the peace process. He called on Israel to continue negotiations.
He also warned Israel against sending forces into self-rule enclaves set up in parts of the West Bank and most of Gaza under interim accords since the historic 1993 Israel-PLO peace deal.
"We hope Israel respects the borders of the Palestinian Authority, otherwise they will endanger the whole region, pushing everything to a critical situation," Abu Rdainah said.
Israel and the Palestinians agreed this week to resume talks on commitments left over from interim peace accords.
That prompted optimism abroad that negotiations stalled for four months after Israel began building a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem might be back on course.
U.S. President Bill Clinton's peace envoy Dennis Ross was to visit the Middle East on Thursday but Washington postponed his trip to allow Israel to mourn.

A Palestine Liberation Organisation security official said Arafat, who publicly condemned the bombing, had declared a state of emergency in Palestinian areas and ordered the arrest of activists of "extremist groups" including Hamas and Islamic Jihad.
The bombing was the deadliest against Israel since March 1996 and the worst since Netanyahu won election in May 1996 on a pledge to bolster security.
World leaders flooded Israel with condolences as well as pleas that it should not let the bombers bury the peace process.
Egyptain Foreign Minister Amr Moussa urged all sides to keep the peace, saying: "What is important in moments like these is confirmation that the peace process will continue."
The European Union strongly condemned the attack and urged Israelis not to let it derail the peace process.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan described the bombing as "abominable and unfortunate" and appealed to both sides to return to the negotiating table.
France, Britain and Germany coupled their condemnations of the bombings with appeals to keep peace hopes alive.
Israeli President Ezer Weizman, whose position is largely ceremonial, said the ultimate solution to the violence was an enduring peace agreement. "Unless we have peace, it won't stop," he said.
